headline: Dynamic budget beating fixed budget does not imply or guarantee that online pattern adaptation causes the gain
claim: FlexPrefill's reported advantage of dynamic settings over fixed budget does not isolate the effect of per-input sparse-pattern search from the effect of per-head budget allocation.
paper_fact: Results in Figure 4 show that dynamic settings lead to improved performance and a better balance between inference speed and model effectiveness compared to static budget allocation.
premise: Dynamic settings in the ablation change budget allocation; pattern search and budget allocation are coupled in the method, so a dynamic-vs-fixed-budget comparison does not by itself identify which component causes the gain.
inference: The comparison supports dynamic budget allocation but not necessarily the online pattern-selection component as the cause of the improvement.
conditional_consequence: If a fixed pattern with the same dynamic budget matches the gain, the online pattern search may add overhead without a necessary accuracy benefit.
critical_link: A controlled ablation holding budget allocation constant while toggling online pattern search is needed to attribute the gain to pattern adaptation.

The fixed-budget baseline differs only in budget, not pattern
Performance and latency are measured under matched sparsity

headline: Dynamic per-input/per-head sparse prefill does not imply or guarantee lower latency at all context lengths
claim: FlexPrefill's adaptive sparse prefill adds representative-attention, pattern-search, and index-construction work; this does not guarantee a net latency reduction at every sequence length, especially when dense attention is already cheap.
paper_fact: At shorter input lengths, non-attention computation overheads are higher. As input length increases, index search construction time grows, but its percentage gradually decreases.
premise: Sparse selection requires extra passes, sorting, and index construction; at short sequence lengths dense attention is relatively cheap, so fixed overhead can dominate.
inference: Net latency benefit is conditional on context length and workload; reported long-context speedups do not establish speedup at short contexts.
conditional_consequence: If deployed at 4k-8k contexts, the dynamic search overhead may erase or reverse the sparse-compute savings.
critical_link: The link from asymptotic overhead terms to measured latency at a given sequence length.

headline: Causal recency of the last query block does not guarantee representativeness of the whole prompt as context length grows.
claim: The fixed last-block Qhat is justified by causal attention and structured-pattern consistency, but causal recency alone does not ensure that the last block captures middle-context evidence needed for all long-context tasks.
paper_fact: We select the last block_size query vectors, denoted as ˆQ, as a representative subset for subsequent estimation. (p.4)
premise: In causal attention, later queries can see the full context, but their attention distribution is not guaranteed to summarize what earlier or middle queries need; longer contexts increase opportunities for task-relevant evidence to sit outside the last block's focus.
inference: If a task requires middle-context retrieval or reasoning, the last-block proxy may omit keys that earlier queries would attend to, so the sparse pattern/index estimated from Qhat can be biased even though the mechanism is causal.
toy_example: Not a measurement: a needle placed mid-prompt may be attended by an early query but not by the final block, so a last-block-only estimate could skip its key line.
conditional_consequence: If middle-context evidence is important and the last block does not attend to it, using only the last block may become more harmful as context length grows.
critical_link: Qhat determines both the estimated attention distribution and the selected sparse indices; if Qhat's attention misses middle evidence, the resulting sparse computation omits it.

Last-block queries do not attend to that evidence
Sparse index selection depends on Qhat rather than full attention

headline: Block-size insensitivity on RULER does not imply or guarantee block-size insensitivity for all tasks, models, or rare-token attention.
claim: The paper's 64-vs-128 block-size ablation on RULER supports flexible block-size choice in tested settings, but it does not establish that pooling granularity is harmless for every model, task, context length, or rare-token retrieval case.
paper_fact: the block size of sparse attention does not significantly impact model effectiveness
premise: An ablation over a finite set of models, tasks, and two block sizes cannot by itself establish universal invariance; changing block size changes pooling units, JS comparison, and gamma-based block selection together.
inference: Thus the reported block-size insensitivity is evidence for the tested RULER configurations, not a guarantee that any hardware-selected block size preserves accuracy or that rare token-level attention survives coarser pooling.
toy_example: Toy example, not a measurement: a 128-token block may contain one critical token whose individual attention mass is diluted by 127 filler tokens; a 64-token split could isolate it, so block-size effects can be task-dependent even if average RULER scores look flat.
conditional_consequence: If practitioners change block size for hardware reasons outside the tested 64/128 RULER settings, then accuracy on rare-token or high-dependency tasks may change even though the paper reports no significant average effect.
critical_link: The ablation compares only block sizes 64 and 128 on RULER for GLM, Yi, and Qwen (Table 7); it does not test LLaMA in that table, does not stress rare-token retrieval, and does not provide a formal pooling-invariance guarantee.

headline: Meeting a per-query cumulative-attention threshold does not guarantee model-level output fidelity across heads and layers.
claim: The cumulative-attention objective is local to each query/head; satisfying gamma does not ensure that compounded attention errors across heads and layers preserve task performance.
paper_fact: The general objective for all query positions, as shown in Equation (3), can be obtained by aggregating the objectives for individual query positions (Equation (8)) across all i ∈[n]
premise: Attention heads and layers interact nonlinearly; local per-head error bounds do not automatically compose into a global model-output bound.
inference: A per-head gamma can preserve selected mass while still allowing correlated errors that degrade long-context task accuracy, especially at high sparsity or long sequences.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): two heads each meet gamma but their output errors point in the same direction, so the combined error is larger than either local error.
conditional_consequence: If head errors are correlated or downstream layers amplify them, gamma tuning may not predict model accuracy; if errors are independent or small, local mass may suffice.
critical_link: The critical link is aggregation from per-query/per-head objectives to the model's final output and benchmark score.
necessary_conditions: Per-head/per-query errors compose with bounded amplification through layers.
Attention heads and layers are approximately independent or errors cancel.
The benchmark metric is smooth in attention-output perturbations.
defeaters: RULER and InfiniteBench results show preserved performance for tested models.
Minimum budget and retained first/last key blocks mitigate head collapse.
Dynamic per-head budgets improve over fixed budgets in the paper's ablations.
do_not_infer: Do not infer the paper claims a global model-output guarantee.
Do not infer per-query thresholds are useless.
Do not infer head coupling is always harmful.
lens: L4/L7: per-query aggregation and scaling to model-level fidelity

mechanism: Attention heads and layers interact nonlinearly; local per-head error bounds do not automatically compose into a global model-output bound. A per-head gamma can preserve selected mass while still allowing correlated errors that degrade long-context task accuracy, especially at high sparsity or long sequences.
